modules.title: Arrays
objectives: Explain shifting during insertion and deletion
modules.complexity: Index access/update O(1); insertion/deletion O(n); storage O(n).
modules.invariant: Valid indices lie in [0,n); insert permits index n. Shifts preserve the order of other elements.
modules.explanation: An array keeps values in indexed slots. Access reads a slot; update replaces it. Inserting opens a slot by shifting right, while deletion closes a gap by shifting left.

question.prompt: What is the worst-case time to insert at the beginning of an array?
question.explanation: Every existing element may need to shift one slot.

modules.title: Linear search
modules.invariant: All indices before the cursor have been checked; the first match is returned.
modules.explanation: Linear search checks each element in order. It works on unsorted inputs and stops at the first equal value.

question.prompt: Which duplicate does this linear search return?
question.explanation: The scan stops immediately at the first equal value.

modules.title: Binary search
modules.complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) extra space.
modules.invariant: If a target is present, it remains in the inclusive [lo,hi] interval.
modules.explanation: Binary search compares the midpoint of an ascending array, discarding the half that cannot contain the target. Any matching duplicate may be returned. Unsorted inputs are rejected.
modules.example: For target 7, compare 5, then 7; return index 3.

question.prompt: What prerequisite does binary search need?
question.explanation: Only ordering justifies discarding half of the remaining interval.

modules.title: Insertion sort
modules.complexity: O(n²) worst/average time, O(n) best time, O(1) extra space.
modules.invariant: Before iteration i, the prefix [0,i) is sorted. Equal elements are not shifted past one another.
modules.explanation: Take a key from the unsorted suffix, shift larger prefix values right, then place the key. It is stable and adapts to nearly sorted inputs.

question.prompt: Why does this insertion sort preserve equal-value order?
options: It shifts only strictly larger values
question.explanation: The strict greater-than comparison leaves existing equal values before the key.

modules.title: Merge sort
modules.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space.
modules.invariant: Each pass merges adjacent sorted runs of width w into sorted runs of width 2w.
modules.explanation: Bottom-up merge sort merges runs of increasing width. Ties choose from the left run, preserving stability. Buffer reads and array writes are separate events.

question.prompt: How much auxiliary space does this merge sort use?
question.explanation: A temporary buffer holds values from each merged run.

modules.title: Quicksort
modules.complexity: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst time; O(n) bounded explicit range stack.
modules.invariant: Within a partition, values before the boundary are ≤ pivot; later scanned values are > pivot.
modules.explanation: An iterative Lomuto partition uses the final value as pivot and an explicit range stack. Equal values go left. This version is not stable; sorted or equal inputs can be quadratic.

question.prompt: Which input can cause quadratic behavior with a final-element pivot?
question.explanation: A final-element pivot on ordered data can repeatedly produce a highly unbalanced partition.

modules.title: Singly linked list
modules.complexity: O(n) indexed insert/delete/search/traverse; O(1) relinking after the predecessor is located. O(n) space.
modules.invariant: The head reaches each active node once; the last next ID is 0 (null). Node IDs remain stable during an operation.
modules.explanation: A singly linked list stores nodes joined by next links. Insert/delete use an index; search returns the first matching node ID. IDs represent conceptual identity, never browser addresses.

question.prompt: Which link changes when inserting after an existing node?
question.explanation: The new node points to the old successor and the predecessor points to the new node.

modules.title: Stack
modules.invariant: The top is the last occupied element; only the top is removed.
modules.explanation: A stack adds and removes values at one end. This release uses an array-backed stack, rejects underflow and caps capacity at 32.

modules.title: Queue
objectives: Distinguish ADT behavior from implementation cost
modules.complexity: Enqueue/inspect O(1); dequeue O(n) in this compact shifting implementation; O(n) storage.
modules.invariant: The front is index 0; dequeue preserves the relative order of the remaining values.
modules.explanation: A queue appends at the back and removes from the front. This teaching implementation shifts on dequeue; a circular-buffer extension can make dequeue constant time.

question.prompt: Which value leaves a FIFO queue first?
question.explanation: First-in-first-out removes the earliest enqueued value.

modules.title: Binary search tree
objectives: Delete leaf, one-child and two-child nodes
modules.complexity: Search/insert/delete O(h); traversals O(n). h may be n in an unbalanced tree; O(n) storage.
modules.invariant: All left descendants are strictly smaller and all right descendants strictly larger. Duplicate inserts are ignored.
modules.explanation: BSTs follow comparisons down the tree. Two-child deletion transplants the inorder successor, preserving node IDs. Traversals visit left/node/right (inorder), node/left/right (preorder), or left/right/node (postorder).
modules.example: Deleting root 8 transplants successor 10; inorder stays sorted.

question.prompt: Which traversal lists BST values in ascending order?
question.explanation: Inorder visits the smaller subtree, the node, then the larger subtree.

modules.title: Graph editor
objectives: Keep stable node and edge IDs
modules.complexity: Adjacency-matrix edge lookup O(1); node removal O(V²); space O(V²).
modules.invariant: Node IDs are unique; undirected edges are symmetric. Parallel edges replace their previous weight; self-loops are allowed.
modules.explanation: Build a graph with at most 16 vertices. Node IDs range from 1 to 31. Edges use integer weights, including zero; direction is explicit. Graph edits are executed by the C engine.
modules.example: An undirected edge 1—2 is traversable from either endpoint.

question.prompt: What does an undirected edge mean?
options: Travel is possible in both directions
Only the smaller ID can be the source
question.explanation: The C adjacency matrix stores both directions.

modules.title: Breadth-first search
modules.complexity: O(V²) with this adjacency matrix; O(V) frontier/visited space.
modules.invariant: Vertices are marked on enqueue, so each reachable vertex enters the queue once.
modules.explanation: BFS visits the source, then its neighbors, then the next layer. It follows outgoing edges in directed graphs and ignores weights. Unreachable vertices are not visited.

question.prompt: Which structure manages the BFS frontier?
question.explanation: A FIFO queue visits earlier layers before later ones.

modules.title: Depth-first search
objectives: Inspect a stack of active vertices
modules.complexity: O(V²) with this adjacency matrix; O(V) explicit stack space.
modules.invariant: Each active stack path follows graph edges; marked vertices are never entered twice.
modules.explanation: DFS uses an explicit stack and a per-vertex neighbor cursor. It descends to the first unvisited outgoing neighbor in input order, then backtracks. Weights are ignored.

options: When the current vertex has no unvisited outgoing neighbors
After every edge regardless of state
Only when every graph vertex is reachable
question.explanation: DFS returns to the parent after exhausting the current vertex’s unvisited neighbors.

modules.title: Dijkstra shortest paths
objectives: Explain why negative weights are rejected
modules.complexity: O(V²) time using linear minimum selection; O(V) distance/visited space.
modules.invariant: The selected unsettled vertex has minimum tentative distance. With nonnegative edges its distance is final.
modules.explanation: Dijkstra computes shortest distances from a source using nonnegative integer weights. Zero-weight edges are supported. Unreachable vertices retain infinity. All negative edges are rejected, including unreachable ones.
modules.example: With 1→2 weight 2, 2→3 weight 1, 1→3 weight 7, distances are 0,2,3.

options: They cannot be stored as integers
question.explanation: A later path through a negative edge could improve an already settled vertex.
